text: Clive John Derby-Lewis (22 January 1936 – 3 November 2016) was a South African politician who initially joined the National Party and later served in the Conservative Party after its split from the National Party in 1982 due to a softening of apartheid policies. He served as a town councillor for Bedfordview (1972–1977), Deputy Mayor (1973–1974), and Mayor (1974–1975), and was made a Freeman of the Johannesburg Mini-Council. He represented Edenvale, Gauteng, on the Transvaal Provincial Council (1972–1981), where he was the National Party spokesman for Education and Hospital Services, and served on various boards including hospitals, primary and high schools, and a school for physically challenged children. He was a founder member of the Conservative Party, serving on its General Council, Parliamentary Caucus, and Transvaal Party Council, including its Information and Financial Committee. After losing his seat in the 1989 election, he was appointed to the State President's Council, where he served on the Economic Affairs and Amenities Committees. He visited London twice as part of a Conservative Party delegation, including in June 1989, and joined the Western Goals Institute as an honorary Vice-President, participating in the 22nd World Anti-Communist League Conference in Brussels in July 1990. Derby-Lewis was known for racially inflammatory remarks, such as claiming in Parliament in 1989 that "If AIDS stops Black population growth it will be like Father Christmas" and remarking "What a pity" about a black man on a runway, which he later apologised for. He was described as a "right-wing extremist" by The Daily Telegraph and as a "rabid racist" by journalist John Carlin. In October 1993, he was convicted of conspiracy to murder Chris Hani, the leader of the South African Communist Party, and sentenced to death, a sentence later reduced to life imprisonment when capital punishment was abolished in 1995. He confessed to his role in the assassination during his amnesty application to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, stating it was encouraged or sanctioned by senior Conservative Party leaders and that he acted "in defence of my people, who were threatened with a Communist take-over," citing his Christian faith in the Afrikaanse Protestant Church as central to his actions. His amnesty application was denied in April 1999, and in 2000, the Cape High Court dismissed an appeal to overturn the decision. Derby-Lewis applied for parole in June 2010, citing his age over 70 and having served more than 15 years, and was denied medical parole in 2011, 2013, and 2015. His medical parole was granted on 29 May 2015 by a judge, and he was released in June 2015 after serving 22 years due to terminal lung cancer. He died from the disease on 3 November 2016. Born in Cape Town, Derby-Lewis had German and Scots ancestry and grew up in Kimberley, being educated at the then-Christian Brothers' College. He worked as a chartered accountant, served as an extraordinary minister of Holy Communion at Blessed Sacrament Church in Johannesburg before leaving the Catholic Church in the early 1980s, and later joined the Afrikaanse Protestantse Kerk, a staunch supporter of apartheid. He spent nineteen years as a volunteer in the South African Citizen Force and became the youngest ever commanding officer of the Witwatersrand Rifles Regiment, affiliated with the Cameronians, earning the John Chard Medal for meritorious service. He married Gaye Derby-Lewis, a former nun from Australia, in 1986, which was his second marriage, and had three children from his first marriage. He was the only member of the Conservative Party Parliamentary Caucus to have served in all four levels of government in South Africa. During his time in Parliament, he was opposed by the Progressive Federal Party, and in March 1988, opposition leader Harry Schwarz called him the "biggest racist in Parliament." He was also a member of the Standing Committees on Provincial Affairs of Natal and Trade and Commerce, and served as Chief Spokesman on Economic Affairs, Technology and Mineral Affairs when the Conservative Party became the Official Opposition. A list of senior ANC and South African Communist Party figures, allegedly developed by Arthur Kemp and including Nelson Mandela and Joe Slovo, was reportedly used in the planning of Hani's assassination. Derby-Lewis had abetted Janusz Waluś, a Polish immigrant, by delivering him the gun used in the assassination on 10 April 1993. His representative advocate, Roelof du Plessis, stated that the medical parole advisory board found his lung cancer to be stage 3b with probable or inconclusive spread to the left adrenal glands, inoperable, with marginal response to treatment and poor prognostic features.
